Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 1–4:

﴿By the star when it sets﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first is that it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), because the name "star" (al-najm) has come to be applied to it predominantly. The meaning of "sets" (hawa) is that it sets and is scattered on the Day of Resurrection. The second is that it refers to the category of stars in general, and the meaning of "sets" is as we have mentioned, or that it shoots forth, pelting the devils (tarjum al-shayatin). The third is that it refers to the stars of the Qur'an, meaning the portions (jumla) that are sent down, and "sets" in this case means "descends."

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾. This is the answer to the oath. The address is to the Quraysh, and "your companion" is the Prophet (ﷺ). He is thus cleared of straying (al-dalal) and error (al-ghayy). The difference between the two is that straying (al-dalal) occurs without intention, whereas error (al-ghayy) occurs with intention and deliberate pursuit.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾, that is, he does not speak according to his own whim and appetite, but only speaks what Allah reveals to him.

﴿It is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

It is also said to mean Allah, Exalted. The first view is more likely, because of His saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 20]. "Al-Quwa" is the plural of "quwwa" (power).

﴿ذُو مِرَّةٍ﴾ means possessor of power. It is also said to mean one of good form. The first meaning is the correct one in the language.

﴿فَٱسْتَوَىٰ﴾ means that Jibril stood firm in the air, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him while he was at Hira'. It is also said that the meaning of "istawa" is that he appeared in his true form, with six hundred wings, having filled the horizon. This was unlike the forms in which he used to appear when he descended with revelation. He mostly descended in the form of the Companion Dihya al-Kalbi.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 9:

﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths, or nearer.﴾ Al-qab (القاب): the measure of the distance, meaning that Jibril was, in nearness to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), the measure of two Arab bow-lengths. Its meaning is from the tip of the bow to its other tip. It was said: from the string to the bow's grip. It was also said: it is not the bow with which one shoots, but a cubit by which measures are gauged, related by al-Tha'labi, who said that it is from the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The sense of the statement is: the distance of Jibril from our master Muhammad (ﷺ) was like the measure of "two bow-lengths." Then these genitive constructions were elided. The meaning of ﴿or nearer﴾ is "or closer." The ﴿or﴾ here is like His saying: ﴿or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. Among the most likely interpretations of it is that when a human looks at him, it is possible in his view that it is two bow-lengths or that it is nearer. What we have mentioned, that these preceding pronouns refer to Jibril, is the correct view, and this has been reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a sound hadith. It was also said that they refer to God Most High, but this view is refuted by the hadith and by reason, since it is obligatory to declare God exempt from those attributes of drawing near, descending, and the like.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 10:

﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Regarding these pronouns there are three opinions. The first is that the meaning is: Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad (ﷺ) what He revealed. The second is: Allah revealed to His servant Jibril (Gabriel) what He revealed, and the pronoun refers to Allah in both of these opinions, because the context of the discourse requires that, even though no mention of Him has preceded it. It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. The third is: Jibril revealed to Allah's servant Muhammad what he revealed, and in His saying ﴿what He revealed﴾ there is an intended ambiguity that calls for magnification and glorification.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verses 11–15:

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ That is, the heart of Muhammad ﷺ did not lie about what he saw with his eyes; rather, his heart affirmed that what he saw with his eyes was true. The one he saw was Jibril, namely when he saw him in his true form, filling the horizon. It was also said that he saw the malakut (dominion) of the heavens and the earth. The first view is more preponderant, due to His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent.﴾ It was also said that the one he saw was Allah, Exalted is He; but ʿAʾishah denied this, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "It is light; how could I see it?" ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ This is an address to the Quraysh, and the meaning is: Will you argue with him about what he sees? The Quraysh had denied when he said that he had seen what he had seen. ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent.﴾ That is, Muhammad certainly saw Jibril, peace and blessings be upon them both, another time, which was the night of the Isra'. It was also said that the pronoun of the object refers to Allah, Exalted is He; ʿAʾishah denied this and said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord on the night of the Isra' has greatly slandered Allah, Exalted is He."

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary.﴾ It is a tree in the seventh heaven. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Its fruit is like the large jars, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants." It was named the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) because the knowledge of every knower ends at it, and none knows what is beyond it except Allah, Exalted is He. It was also said that it was so named because the command of Allah that descends meets at it; the angels of the heights do not pass beyond it downward, and the angels of the lowest realm do not pass beyond it upward. ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge.﴾ That is, the Garden that Allah promised His servants is the Garden of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha)—the Garden of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa). It was also said that it is another garden where the spirits of the martyrs take refuge; the first view is more apparent and more well known.

When the lote-tree was being covered by that which covered it. There is vagueness here, intended to express magnification. Ibn Mas'ud said: "It was covered by golden moths (fara sh min dhahab)." It was also said: "the multitude of angels." And in a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It was covered by colours I do not know what they are." This is the more appropriate way to interpret the verse: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. That is, the sight of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) did not swerve from the wonders he saw; rather, he affirmed them and was certain of them. ﴿Nor did it transgress﴾: that is, it did not go beyond what he saw to something else.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 18:

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. That is, what he saw on the night of the Isra' (the night journey) of the heavens, Paradise, Hell, the angels, the prophets, and other things. It is possible that al-Kubra (the greatest) is an object (maf'ul) or an attribute (na't) of "signs of his Lord," and the meaning differs according to this.

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ These are idols that were worshipped besides Allah. So Allah addressed the Arabs who worshipped them, in a manner of rebuke to them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The seeing here is ru'yat al-'ayn (seeing with the eye), because the idols mentioned are visible bodies. As for al-Lat, it was an idol in al-Ta'if, and it was said that it was in the Ka'bah. As for al-'Uzza, it was a rock in al-Ta'if, and it was said that it was a tree. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down, and there came out from it a female devil (shaytanah), with her hair disheveled, calling out "woe!" So he struck her with the sword until he killed her. It was also said that it was a house that the Arabs revered. The original form of the word al-'Uzza is the feminine of al-a'azz (the most mighty). As for Manat, it was a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, between Makkah and Madinah. And it was the greatest of these idols.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: For this reason Allah said "the third, the other," and He emphasized it with these two attributes. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Ukhra" (the other) is a term of blame and contempt, meaning the one that comes later, the lowly in rank.

From the same usage is the verse: ﴿Each later group said to its predecessor...﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ These are idols that were worshipped besides Allah. So Allah addressed the Arabs who worshipped them, in a manner of rebuke to them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The seeing here is ru'yat al-'ayn (seeing with the eye), because the idols mentioned are visible bodies. As for al-Lat, it was an idol in al-Ta'if, and it was said that it was in the Ka'bah. As for al-'Uzza, it was a rock in al-Ta'if, and it was said that it was a tree. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down, and there came out from it a female devil (shaytanah), with her hair disheveled, calling out "woe!" So he struck her with the sword until he killed her. It was also said that it was a house that the Arabs revered. The original form of the word al-'Uzza is the feminine of al-a'azz (the most mighty). As for Manat, it was a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, between Makkah and Madinah. And it was the greatest of these idols.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: For this reason Allah said "the third, the other," and He emphasized it with these two attributes. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Ukhra" (the other) is a term of blame and contempt, meaning the one that comes later, the lowly in rank.

From the same usage is the verse: ﴿Each later group said to its predecessor...﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ They used to say: the angels and these idols are daughters of God. So God denounced them for that, meaning: how do you assign to yourselves male offspring, while assigning to God daughters, who are in your eyes lowly and hateful? This same meaning has been mentioned in Surat al-Nahl and elsewhere. It is also possible that He denounced them for making these idols partners with God, Exalted is He, even though they are females, and females are lowly and hateful in their eyes.

**﴿That, then, is an unjust division.﴾** Meaning: this division of yours, in which you have assigned the males to yourselves and the females to God, is unjust and not equitable. The word ḍīzā (ضيزى) is on the pattern fu'lā with the fāʾ vowelled with a ḍammah, but it was given a kasrah because of the yāʾ that follows it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 23:

﴿It is nothing but names that you have named﴾ The pronoun refers to the idols. This meaning was mentioned in al-A'raf [7:71] in His saying: ﴿Do you dispute with me over names﴾ ﴿They follow nothing but assumption﴾ meaning that they utter statements without any proof, like their saying that the angels are daughters of God, and their saying that the idols will intercede for them, and other than that.

﴿Am lil-insani ma tamanna?﴾ [Or does man have whatever he wishes?]

Here "am" (or, rather, a rhetorical denial) is used for denial (inkar), and "al-insan" refers to the human race, the sons of Adam: that is, no one has whatever he wishes; rather the matter is in the hand of God. It was said that the reference is to what the disbelievers hoped for, namely the intercession of the idols; it was said that it refers to the statement of al-As ibn Wa'il: "I will certainly be given wealth and children"; and it was said that it is the wish of some of them to be a prophet. The best interpretation is to take the wording in its general sense.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 26:

﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens﴾ (the verse): a refutation of the disbelievers in their claim that the idols intercede for them, as if he were saying: The noble angels, their intercession avails nothing except by the permission of Allah, so how [could it be so for] your idols?

﴿Except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾: its meaning is that the angels do not intercede for anyone except after Allah has given them permission to intercede on his behalf and is pleased with him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verses 27–28:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females﴾. It means their saying that the angels are daughters of Allah. Then He refuted them with His saying: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verses 27–28:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females﴾. It means their saying that the angels are daughters of Allah. Then He refuted them with His saying: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾.

﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾: meaning, their knowledge ends there, because they did what benefits them in this world and did not know what benefits them in the Hereafter. ﴿That He may recompense﴾: the lam (the particle of purpose) is connected to the sense of what precedes it, and the implied sense is: "Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did." It was also said that it is connected to "went astray and was guided." ﴿The major sins of the sin﴾: we have mentioned the major sins in Surat al-Nisa' [31]. ﴿Except the lamam﴾: concerning it there are four opinions. The first: that it refers to minor sins, so the exception on this view is disjunct (munqati', an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it). Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 53, verses 33–34:

﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ (the verse): It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It is also said that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. ﴿And gave little and withheld﴾ means he cut off giving and held back.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 53, verses 33–34:

﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ (the verse): It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It is also said that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. ﴿And gave little and withheld﴾ means he cut off giving and held back.

﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his commitments]﴾. It was said: [he fulfilled them] in obedience to God by sacrificing his son. It was said: [he fulfilled them] in conveying the message. It was said: [he fulfilled them] in the laws of Islam. It was said: [he fulfilled them] in the words with which God tested him. It was said: [he fulfilled] these ten verses.

﴿Let no bearer of burdens bear the burden of another﴾ has been mentioned earlier. This sentence explains what is in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both.

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾. Here, *al-sa'y* (السعي) means action. Its apparent meaning is that no one benefits from the deeds of another. This verse is evidence for Malik's position that no one fasts on behalf of a deceased guardian who owed fasts. Scholars agree that financial acts, such as charity and freeing a slave, may be performed by a person on behalf of another, and their benefit reaches the one on whose behalf they are done. They differ regarding physical acts such as prayer and fasting. It has been said that this verse is abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by His words: ﴿And We will join them with their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. The correct view is that it is *muhkam* (definitive, not abrogated), because it is a report, and reports are not abrogated.

There are three explanations of its meaning. The first: it is a report about what was the case in the law of other nations, so it does not bind us in our law. The second: a person has what he himself did with right, and he also has what another did on his behalf by the gift of the doer. So the verse establishes the basic reality and not what goes beyond it. The third: it refers to sins. There is agreement that no one bears another's sin, and the verse's following words support this: ﴿Let no bearer of burdens bear the burden of another﴾. It is as if He is saying: no one is held to account for the sin of another, and no one is held to account except for his own sin.

﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that creation will see it on the Day of Resurrection. The more evident view is that the one who did it will see it, based on His words: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 42:

﴿And that to your Lord is the final end.﴾ On this there are two opinions. The first is that its meaning is that the return in the Hereafter is to God. The second is that its meaning is that knowledge ends with God, and then the scholars stop at that point. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no reflection upon the Lord."

And that it is He who makes [people] laugh and makes [them] weep.

It has been said: its meaning is that He makes the people of Paradise laugh and makes the people of the Fire weep, but this is a specification for which there is no evidence. It has also been said: He makes the sky weep with rain and makes the earth laugh with plants, but this is a metaphor (majaz). And it has been said: He created in the children of Adam laughter and weeping. The correct view is that it is an expression for joy and sorrow, because laughter is an indication of gladness and joy, just as weeping is an indication of sorrow. So the meaning is that Allah the Exalted saddens whomever He wills of His servants and gladdens whomever He wills.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 44:

﴿And that He causes death and gives life﴾. He means the well-known life and the well-known death. It has also been said: He gives life through faith and causes death through disbelief. The first is the stronger view, because it is the literal meaning.

﴿from a drop of semen﴾, meaning the seminal fluid, ﴿when it is emitted﴾, from your saying: the man "amnā" (emitted) when the seminal fluid came out of him. ﴿the second creation﴾, meaning the re-creation for the gathering (ḥashr, the assembling of people on the Day of Resurrection). ﴿and He enriches﴾, meaning He grants His servants wealth, and it derives from qunyat al-māl (the possession of property), which is its acquisition and storing. It was said that the meaning of ﴿aqnā﴾ is "He impoverishes", but the language does not require this. It was also said that its meaning is "He pleases", and it was said that it means "He makes His servant content." ﴿Al-Shi'rā﴾ is a star in the sky, and it is called Kalb al-Jabbār (the Dog of the Mighty One). There are two Sha'rās: al-Ghumayṣā' and al-'Abūr. He singled it out for mention, apart from the rest of the stars, because some of the Arabs used to worship it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 50–54:

﴿ʿĀdan al-ūlā﴾ He described them as "the first" because they were in ancient times; they are the first in relation to the later nations. It has also been said that they were called "the first" because there is another, later ʿĀd, but this does not hold. Nāfiʿ recited ﴿ʿādan lūlā﴾, assimilating the tanwin of ʿād into the lām of al-ūlā, dropping the hamza and transferring its vowel to the lām. Al-Muzanī and al-Mubarrad criticised this reading as weak. Qālūn pronounced the hamza of al-ūlā, unlike Warsh. The rest recited according to the original form, with the tanwin of ʿādan kasra'd and the lām of al-ūlā sukūn-ed. ﴿Wa-Thamūda fa-mā abqā﴾, meaning He left none of them remaining. It has also been said: He did not leave anything upon them. ﴿Wal-Mu'tafikata ahwā * Fa-ghashshāhā mā ghashshā﴾. It is the city of the people of Lūṭ. The meaning of ahwā is that He overturned it from above to below. In His saying "what covered them" is a magnifying of the matter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 55:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ This is an address to mankind in general. Its meaning: "Which of your Lord's blessings do you doubt?"

Translation:

﴿This is a warner from the warners of old﴾. He means the Qur'an, or the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning of "from the warners of old" is: from the same kind and character as the earlier warnings.
﴿The Imminent One has drawn near﴾, meaning: the Resurrection has drawn near.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 53, verse 58:

﴿Kashifah﴾ (lit. "uncovering" / "disclosing") – its wording may carry three possible readings. It may be a verbal noun (maṣdar), like ʿāfiyah (well-being), meaning: there is no uncovering (kashf) for it. It may be in the sense of the active participle (kāshif), with the feminine ending (tā') for emphasis (mubālaghah), as in ʿallāmah (one who knows very much). And it may be an adjective (ṣifah) of an elided noun, the estimated phrase being: "a soul that uncovers" (nafs kāshifah) or "a group that uncovers" (jamāʿah kāshifah).

Its meaning may also bear two interpretations. The first is that it derives from kashf in the sense of removal (izālah), meaning: there is no one to remove it when it occurs. The second is that it means knowledge (iṭṭilāʿ), meaning: there is no one who knows its time except Allah.
﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾ The reference is to the Qur'an, and their wondering at it is their denial of it.

"And you are amusing yourselves" — that is, playing and heedless. It is said: neglectful and remiss.

Wait, I need to be precise. The passage in Arabic is short; here is a faithful translation:

﴿وَأَنتُمْ سَامِدُونَ﴾ — "while you are sāmidūn" (in the Qur'anic text: ﴿and you are sāmidūn﴾). That is, lāʿibūn lāhūn (playing and heedless). It is also said: ghāfilūn mufarriṭūn (neglectful and remiss).

ﷻ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾. This is a place of prostration according to al-Shafi'i and others. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it, prostrated, and everyone who was with him prostrated.
